dossier.orientation: Buttondown is a hosted newsletter platform whose documented HTTP API and outbound webhooks let a developer manage subscribers and react to newsletter events from their own code instead of its web dashboard.

unverified_requirement_basis.A documented API endpoint for composing,: Automate newsletter operations end-to-end via an API so newsletter sending integrates with existing tools

defining_need_fit.caveat: The selected evidence documents API availability on all plans, a 600 requests/minute global limit, a 100/day subscriber-creation cap with a bulk-import fallback, and outbound webhooks, but no send-or-draft endpoint; CRM, Slack, GitHub and Sheets are reached through the API, webhooks or Zapier rather than documented native connectors (R7), which the stated need does not itself require.
defining_need_fit.why: Programmatic subscriber management and event-driven triggers are documented, but the sending half of "end-to-end via an API" is not established by the selected evidence.

ranked_relevance.why: The API being available on all plans including free is the load-bearing fact for an operator who chose the API over paid built-in automation on budget grounds.
A documented 600 requests/minute global ceiling states what the API mechanism actually allows for script- and cron-driven use.
Outbound webhooks are the documented mechanism by which an external application reacts to newsletter events, with Slack notification as the documentation's own example.
The 100/day cap on POST /v1/subscribers is the documented exception to the general API limit and bounds programmatic subscriber onboarding.
Documents the supported bulk path when the subscriber-creation cap is hit, and that no separate batch-create API is described.
States the actual shape of Buttondown's integration surface: broader tools are reached via the API or Zapier, not via documented native CRM, Slack, GitHub or Sheets connectors.
The required capability fact that the API is rate-limited but generous for most use cases, though the wording is unquantified and R3/R4 carry the numbers.
Emailing a post in to send or draft is a documented non-server, non-dashboard path relevant to an operator unwilling to maintain infrastructure.
Free for the first 100 subscribers bounds the cost of a hobby-scale evaluation of the API.
The one-email-a-day pricing assumption is the explicit condition on any automated sending cadence built against the API.
CSV import carrying tags, metadata and notes describes the bulk path's data shape but is a dashboard mechanism, not API automation.
Only email address being required narrows what a bulk import must supply; background to the import fallback.

CSV-plus-Markdown email export is a dashboard-initiated mechanism unrelated to the stated automation need.
Custom hosting domain for archives is a paid-plan DNS setup unrelated to API-driven sending.
Free concierge migration matters to a switcher, and this audience is defined by how it operates rather than by migrating.
True and licensed, but a content-policy clause tells an API-driven operator nothing about the task and reads as a restriction.
Team review before send is licensed but poorly matched to a solo or hobby operator driving sends from code.
Role separation around API keys presumes a staffed team this audience's researched situation does not show.
No surcharge on paid subscribers is licensed but irrelevant to automating operations via an API.
Sponsorship revenue share is licensed but off-task for this audience's stated need.

dossier.orientation: Buttondown is hosted newsletter software that imports an existing Substack list, sends to it, serves the archive on the writer's own domain, and lets the writer download the whole archive as Markdown plus CSV at any time.

setup_conditions: Upload a CSV whose columns Buttondown recognises or that are manually mapped; only the email address column is required (R8, R9)
Optionally hand the list to Buttondown's free concierge migration instead of importing it yourself (E3)

Email posts in from the address used to join Buttondown to send or draft them (E9)
Start the archive export from the Emails tab in the dashboard (R1)

defining_need_fit.caveat: Import, sending, custom-domain archive hosting and a full Markdown+CSV archive export are all documented, but the archive is still served through Buttondown's servers via CNAME rather than self-hosted, Buttondown's own terms impose a content policy, and the export doc does not address ownership, retention or licence terms over the exported content.
defining_need_fit.why: Every mechanical component of moving and running the newsletter is documented, while the stated ownership-outright and outside-platform-moderation conditions are not established by the selected evidence.

ranked_relevance.why: Downloading a CSV plus a folder of each email's contents is the documented mechanism closest to the stated wish to hold the archive themselves.
Serving archives at newsletter.example.com rather than buttondown.com/username is the documented answer to the own-domain hosting part of the workflow.
A free concierge migration regardless of list size addresses the move itself for a solo writer with no ops help.
States what the import actually carries over — subscribe date, tags, metadata, notes — which is the mechanism behind the list move.
Documents the import's only hard requirement and the optionality of the rest, bounding what a Substack CSV must contain.
Emailing a post in from the joining address documents the sending path after the move.
Free for the first 100 subscribers makes an ordinary-volume evaluation possible before committing the list.
Buttondown's own content policy is the documented limit on the audience's wish to sit outside platform moderation, so it bounds claims rather than licensing them.

problem_fits.caveat: The import names subscribe date, tags, metadata and notes but not engagement metrics or consent records, and the selected evidence establishes no accuracy or reconciliation guarantee for subscriber counts.
problem_fits.why: Documented import, free concierge migration and full archive export give the writer their own copies, but nothing in the ledger proves counts reconcile or that stewardship complaints are answered.

problem_fits.caveat: Buttondown's terms prohibit hosting material advocating violence against protected classes, malicious impersonation and IP infringement, and are revisable at any time; the ledger contains no Substack policy text for comparison and says nothing about social-feed or follow-style growth mechanics.
problem_fits.why: Buttondown publishes a content policy covering the hateful-content concern, but no comparison with Substack and no statement about algorithmic growth mechanics is established by the selected evidence.

segment_objections.objection: A custom hosting domain is not self-hosting — the archive still runs on Buttondown's servers.
segment_objections.answer: Documented: the hosting domain is a CNAME to custom-domains.buttondown.com on the Standard plan, and the Emails tab export downloads a CSV plus a folder containing the contents of each email, so the writer can keep their own copy.

segment_objections.objection: Moving does not escape content moderation, since Buttondown imposes its own policy.
segment_objections.answer: Buttondown's terms state what is prohibited — advocating violence against protected classes, malicious impersonation, IP infringement — and nothing in the selected evidence compares that with any other platform's policy.
